final.title: When AI scope starts to wander, draw the box first
final.body:
Early signs of unbounded scope usually show up when one workflow starts collecting every adjacent problem.

If you are a small-business owner, the first question is simple: what is the one recurring job you want to automate? Not the whole business. One job.

For example, “respond to customer emails” is a workflow. “Improve customer satisfaction” is not. The difference matters because a broad goal has no clear input, decision rule, or output. A bounded workflow does.

Before you ask whether AI fits, draw the box in plain English:
- what comes in
- what decision is made
- what goes out
- what is explicitly out of scope

Then check three things. Are the decisions mostly rule-based? Do you have enough past examples to show the pattern? Can a wrong answer be caught before it reaches a customer? If the answer is yes, the workflow may be a fit. If not, it probably needs restructuring first, or it may be better handled by hiring.

One practical next step: write down the workflow in that format and stop there. If you cannot define the boundary, the scope is already wandering.

final.title: When AI scope starts to wander, draw the box first
final.body:
If you are an owner-operator, the first sign of unbounded scope is usually not a technical failure. It is a workflow that starts as one repeatable task and then quietly turns into three.

Use a simple rule: before you call something an AI project, write down the boundary in plain English. What is the one recurring workflow? What input starts it? What output ends it? And what is explicitly out of scope?

For example, "respond to customer emails" is a workflow. "Improve customer satisfaction" is not. The first can be bounded. The second opens the door to every exception in the business.

A second check is the approval gate. If the workflow touches money movement, legal commitments, or other high-risk decisions, human approval stays in the loop. That is not a nice-to-have; it is the box.

If the request keeps adding new systems, new approvals, or extra exceptions before the first version is defined, the scope is already wandering. Stop there. Write the boundary down first, then decide whether the workflow is bounded enough to automate, better restructured, or better left to a hire.
